title: The Curse of Dimensionality 🧙‍♂️
description: Understand why too many features can break models and how to think geometrically about high‑dimensional space.

slides.title: When More Features Hurt 😵
slides.content:
# The Curse of Dimensionality

Intuitively, more features should mean more information. But in machine learning, adding too many features can make data **sparse**, distances meaningless, and models overfit.

- **Sparsity**: in high dimensions, the same number of data points covers the space very thinly. Imagine 10 points in a line (dense) vs 10 points in a room (sparse).
- **Distance breakdown**: in high dimensions, distances between points become similar; the concept of “nearest neighbour” loses meaning.
- **Computational cost**: training time often grows with feature count.

This is why we need **dimensionality reduction** and **feature selection**.

slides.title: Geometric Intuition 📐
slides.content:
# Volume Moves to the Edges

Consider a unit cube in d dimensions. As d grows, almost all the volume concentrates in the corners. A sphere inscribed in the cube becomes a tiny fraction of the cube’s volume.

This means data tends to be far from the centre; distances become uniformly large. Clustering and nearest‑neighbour methods suffer.

A practical rule: for many algorithms, the number of training examples should be at least 5‑10 times the number of features. If you have 10,000 features and 1,000 samples, you're in trouble.

quizData.question: What happens to nearest‑neighbour distances as dimensionality increases?
quizData.explanation: In high dimensions, the contrast between near and far diminishes; distances tend to a uniform distribution.

slides.title: Fighting the Curse ⚔️
slides.content:
# Dimensionality Reduction Strategies

- **Feature selection**: pick a subset of original features (filter, wrapper, embedded).
- **Feature extraction**: transform features into a lower‑dimensional space (PCA, t‑SNE, autoencoders).
- **Regularisation**: L1 (Lasso) pushes some coefficients to zero, effectively performing feature selection.

All of these help models generalise better, train faster, and sometimes even improve interpretability.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Start Simple
Always try a model with all features first, then systematically remove or transform features. Dimensionality reduction is a tool, not a must‑do in every project.
